doc.title: Michael Max Fleming interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

title: Changes in club work, cabaret law, bass-and-piano jobs and drummers
summary: Work stayed steady as the two-band format faded. Under the cabaret law many jobs were bass and piano, and Mary Lou taught him to get along with drummers.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I saw it when I was playing when the drinking age went up. That affected a lot of the club work also. Were there a period of lean years. I mean you were sort of just talking about that it started to change. Did that became like lean for you? Harder to make a living?

No, not really. The two bands weren’t existing but what happened is things opened up more because, remember before when I first got to New York it was a cabaret law. You couldn’t have drums except in certain places with certain kind of licensing. So and that was just perfect for me. It threw the rabbit in the briar patch or wherever the rabbit got thrown. Because that was my format. My uncle would come by and we would play just bass and piano. So most of the jobs around town were bass and piano. And I know I didn’t — there you go you’re saying, did you depend on the drummer, I didn’t have a drummer. I was the drummer. So that’s for me, I never depend on a drummer. But one thing that I’ve learned, drummers even throw things at me, but I didn’t fight them. With some groups that’s an ongoing thing. “This is mine.” Mary Lou just taught me certain
things about that too, about the drums. The drum is the most domineering instrument. Did you ever see a man riding on an elephant’s back? So there’s things that can be done.

There’s things that could — but some of my best friends are drummers because I’ve been standing near them all my life. Well I’ve got to be a dummy to not understand — you spend a lot of time with drummers I think you’d better learn how to get along with them. I think that’s the way to go. Does that make — that makes sense?
